samples.text:
Nowadays, many people move to live and work in another country. Some people think that immigrants should follow the customs and lifestyle of their new country, while others believe they should keep their own traditions. This essay will discuss both sides before giving my opinion.

On the one hand, there are reasons why immigrants should adapt to the new culture. If they learn the local language and customs, it is more easy for them to find a job and make friends with local people. It also help them to feel part of the community. In addition, local people may be more welcoming if newcomers respect the rules and traditions of the country. If immigrants live in separate groups and do not mix with others, it can cause misunderstanding and conflicts.

On the other hand, many people believe immigrants should keep their own culture. Traditions such as language, food, festivals and religion are part of a person's identity, and it is very difficult to forget them. Also, children of immigrants can learn two cultures and two languages, which is a big advantage for them. Moreover, when different cultures live together, the society become more interesting and diverse. For example, in many big cities people can enjoy food and music from all over the world.

In my opinion, immigrants should do both. They should respect the laws and learn the language of the new country, but they can also keep their traditions at home and in their community. I think this is the best way for everyone to live together peacefully.

In conclusion, adapting to a new culture and keeping traditions are both important. I believe immigrants should find a balance between them.

samples.text:
International migration has made many societies multicultural, raising questions about how newcomers should relate to the culture of their adopted country. Some believe immigrants should embrace local customs, while others think they should preserve their own traditions. In my view, the most successful approach involves a combination of both.

Those who argue for adopting local customs emphasise the importance of integration. Immigrants who learn the language and understand social norms are likely to find employment more easily, build relationships with their neighbours and participate fully in public life. In contrast, communities that remain isolated may face misunderstanding and even hostility from the wider population. From this perspective, adapting to the new way of life is not only practical but also a sign of respect towards the host society.

On the other hand, many people believe that expecting immigrants to abandon their heritage is both unfair and unrealistic. Cultural traditions, including language, religion, cuisine and family customs, are a central part of personal identity, and giving them up can lead to a painful sense of loss. Moreover, the diversity that immigrants bring can enrich the host country, introducing new ideas, foods and festivals. Many of the world's most dynamic cities owe much of their character to generations of migrants who kept their traditions alive.

I believe integration does not require assimilation. Newcomers should respect the laws and core values of their new home and make a real effort to learn the language, as these are essential for living together harmoniously. However, they should also feel free to maintain the traditions that are meaningful to them, and host society should see this diversity as a strength instead of a threat.

In conclusion, although adapting to the local way of life is important for immigrants' success, I believe they should not have to give up their own cultural traditions, and a balance between the two benefits everyone.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant support · logical progression with clear paragraph focus · less common vocabulary (assimilation, heritage) · frequent error-free sentences with one article slip.

samples.text:
As migration reshapes societies around the world, the question of how newcomers should relate to the culture of their adopted country has become increasingly prominent. Some maintain that immigrants ought to adopt the customs and way of life of their new home, while others believe they should retain their own cultural traditions. In my view, this is a false choice: successful integration involves adapting in some respects while preserving one's heritage in others.

The argument for adopting local customs centres on social cohesion and personal opportunity. Newcomers who master the language and understand prevailing norms are far better placed to secure employment, access public services and form friendships beyond their own community. Where migrant groups remain largely separate, mutual suspicion can develop on both sides, fuelling prejudice and limiting social mobility. Adapting to the host culture can therefore be seen as both a practical necessity and a gesture of goodwill.

Those who favour preserving cultural traditions, however, raise equally important points. A person's language, faith, cuisine and customs are deeply bound up with their sense of self, and pressure to abandon them can be alienating, particularly for older migrants. Moreover, cultural diversity is a source of vitality for host societies, enriching their food, arts and ideas; many of the world's most vibrant cities are defined precisely by the traditions that successive waves of migrants have brought with them.

For these reasons, I believe a distinction should be drawn between shared civic foundations and private cultural life. Immigrants should respect the law, embrace fundamental values such as equality, and make a genuine effort to learn the local language, since these form the basis of a common public life. Beyond this, they should be free to maintain the traditions that give their lives meaning, and host societies should welcome rather than merely tolerate them.

In conclusion, rather than choosing between assimilation and separation, immigrants and their new communities benefit most from a balance in which shared civic values coexist with a diversity of cultural traditions.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly developed · sophisticated position that reframes the debate · excellent cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (social cohesion, civic foundations) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
